grand_strategy.reading:
Sri Lanka is a small island on the Indian Ocean sea lanes, and its foreign policy is driven first by money: the IMF programme, creditors, Gulf remittances and fuel imports. The Dissanayake government (NPP, in office since September 2024) tries to turn that position into several deals at once. India gets energy, defence and the grid; China keeps Hambantota and the refinery it has already signed for; the EU and the US keep trade preference and tariff relief in play.
The line it calls neutral is a constraint as much as an instrument. It keeps every lender open, and it is what a debt setback, a fishermen's dispute, a Tamil vote in Geneva or a Gulf oil shock would test first.

stances.note: Transactional cooperation without alignment. Dissanayake's first trip as president (Dec 2024) ended with a pledge that Sri Lankan territory would not be used in ways detrimental to India. The April 2025 visit added a five-year defence umbrella arrangement, a grid interconnection agreement and a trilateral Trincomalee energy hub with the UAE. Not an ally: there is no treaty of alliance and Colombo keeps its neutral line. Cooling pressure comes from the Palk Strait fishermen arrests and from Tamil politics. Bond - affinity: our reading (confidence C), shared Buddhist and cultural ties and the Indian Ocean neighbourhood; no kinship is claimed.

stances.note: Debt-linked cooperation without alignment. Hambantota went under a 99-year lease in July 2017 after Chinese loans. The Sinopec refinery deal was fast-tracked in January 2025 (US$3.7bn, 200,000 barrels a day; work expected in 2025, not confirmed in later reporting). The one-year ban on foreign research vessels lapsed at the end of 2024 without a finished SOP. In 2025 entry was handled case by case: the navy denied the UN-chartered vessel in May and the President approved it in June. That is a lapse, not a formal relaxation. Bond - none: pure interest and debt, our reading (C). The debt figure is not reconciled (about US$6bn in some reports, US$8bn in others).

stances.note: Trade friction managed by negotiation. The US reciprocal tariff on Sri Lankan goods came down from 44% to 20% after talks with the US Trade Representative; the 20% rate took effect on 7 August 2025. Since is the start of the tariff regime, not of the relationship. Adani withdrew a US$553m DFC loan request for the Colombo West terminal in December 2024, after US bribery charges against its chairman; Colombo said it had no objection. An aid-cut premise was not found in the sources and is not recorded. A report of a 10% bracket after a July 2026 forced-labour import ban rests on one explainer and is not recorded. Bond - none: transactional.

stances.note: Cooperates on trade and Commonwealth business but resists the accountability track the UK leads. Resolution 46/1 (2021) created the evidence project. The UK-led text A/HRC/60/L.1/Rev.1 (October 2025) renewed it for two years without a vote; Colombo rejected it, calling its reference to 51/1 an unprecedented, ad hoc expansion of the mandate. The grade is reluctant because the friction is structural (the state's own war record), not a trade quarrel. Bond - affinity: former colonial power and Commonwealth member, our reading (C).
